content: 1. The guidelines involve collaboration among political, managerial, and technical personnel from various ministries responsible for health, energy, environment, development/planning, infrastructure, and forestry. These include agencies focused on testing, standards, and certification, as well as public and private energy production and supply utilities. 2. Health authorities and practitioners engaged in planning and delivering preventive services at national, regional, and local levels are key stakeholders. Multisectoral groups are also involved in developing and implementing country action plans and investment strategies to improve access to cleaner, safer, and more efficient household energy. 3. Development cooperations and international non-governmental organizations (NGOs) are working to enhance access to cleaner, safer, and more efficient household energy. International initiatives, such as the UN Foundation’s Global Alliance for Clean Cookstoves (GACC) and the UN Secretary-General’s Sustainable Energy for All initiative (SE4All), are also contributing to this effort. 4. Researchers focusing on the causes of diseases and the effectiveness of preventive interventions are a primary audience for systematic evidence reviews. These reviews are intended for technical staff and researchers working in fields such as combustion science, emissions, air pollution, environmental health, safety (e.g., burns and poisoning risks), and policy development for the adoption and sustained use of interventions. 5. Best practice recommendations addressing the health and climate impacts of household energy are targeted at policymakers formulating climate change mitigation strategies. This includes partnerships such as the Climate and Clean Air Coalition, which focuses on short-lived climate pollutants resulting from incomplete combustion of household fuels. 6. The guidelines aim to raise awareness of the significant health burden and other impacts associated with current household fuel combustion practices, which have not received adequate attention. 7. The development of these guidelines began with the WHO global update in 2005 on particulate matter, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and sulfur dioxide. A subsequent planning meeting in Bonn in 2006 outlined the framework for indoor air quality guidelines related to household fuel combustion. 8. Following approval of the planning process and the establishment of the WHO Steering Group (SG) and Guidelines Development Group (GDG), a meeting in Geneva in January 2011 defined the scope, topics, and priorities for systematic reviews and evidence collection. 9. The GDG decided that it was unnecessary to review evidence from the published WHO air quality guidelines (AQGs) for air pollutant standards, as these would serve as the basis for the current guidelines. 10. Evidence reviews were commissioned, and drafts underwent external peer review. These were discussed at a main GDG and SG meeting in April 2012 in Delhi, in collaboration with the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR). The scope was finalized, recommendations were drafted, and decision tables were used to determine the strength of the recommendations. 11. Evidence was sought to address scoping questions, including emission rates required to meet air quality guidelines, health risks from household air pollution (HAP), and the impacts of interventions on HAP levels. Barriers to transitioning to improved stoves and clean fuels were also examined. 12. Specific health risks associated with coal and kerosene use were reviewed, including carcinogenicity, toxic contaminants, and constraints on clean combustion. Evidence on kerosene use, pollutant levels, and health impacts was summarized. 13. Systematic reviews also addressed safety concerns, such as risks of burns, scalds, and poisoning from liquid fuels, as well as factors influencing the adoption and sustained use of improved stoves and clean fuels. 14. The guidelines emphasize the synergies between health and climate impacts, highlighting the significant warming effects of inefficient biomass use and emissions from incomplete fuel combustion. 15. Evidence reviews included laboratory testing, epidemiological studies, and policy case studies. The quality of individual studies was assessed using standard methods, ranging from laboratory emission studies to implementation program case studies. 16. Data inconsistencies were reconciled through grouping response data or excluding unreliable data from analysis. The suitability of test protocols for emissions testing and adherence to quality control standards were also evaluated. 17. The guidelines aim to provide a comprehensive synthesis of systematic reviews and other evidence, including modeling approaches for emissions and exposure-response relationships. This ensures robust recommendations for improving household energy practices and reducing associated health and environmental risks.
